design_detail: Narrative review (journal section: Review Article) of the prevalence of use and acute toxicity of NBOMe drugs (N-2-methoxybenzyl analogues of 2C-X phenethylamines), written by two clinical toxicologists of Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust and King's College London (Wood, Dargan) and two staff members of the European Monitoring Centre for Drugs and Drug Addiction (Sedefov, Cunningham) (p. 85). Described search: PubMed with the term 'NBOMe' and the names of ten NBOMe compounds, 1966–2014; abstracts of the 2010–2014 EAPCCT and 2010–2013 NACCT congresses; the EMCDDA's European Information System and Database on New Drugs; a Google search for grey literature; each paper kept if it related to prevalence of use or acute toxicity (pp. 85–86, Methods). No other eligibility criteria, screening procedure, flow of records or appraisal tool is described, and the review is not presented as systematic. Evidence base: 29 published cases of acute toxicity (several only as congress abstracts), 25 cases reported to the EU Early Warning System and 4 deaths from the EMCDDA risk assessment of 25I-NBOMe (April 2014), one poison-centre series (Texas, 25 cases), media and forensic reports of deaths, two 2013 surveys and Erowid and forum counts. Synthesis: case-by-case narrative, noting for each case whether and how the drug was confirmed, with crude pooled percentages of features across the 29 published cases. Filed as a narrative review with the editors' five-domain checklist (METHODS §5.3).
can_establish: What had been published or reported to European agencies by late 2014 about NBOMe poisonings and deaths (which features were recorded, in how many of 29 published cases, in what settings and with what analytical confirmation), how NBOMes were found or sold (mostly on blotters, with several people believing they had taken LSD or 'acid'), and what two 2013 surveys of people who answer a drug survey or go to nightclubs reported about use.
cannot_establish: How often NBOMe use leads to poisoning, seizures or death (published case reports select severe cases and have no denominator); that the NBOMe caused the features in each case (only about half the published cases had the drug found in the patient's own samples, and other drugs were often present); how common NBOMe use is in any population (both surveys are non-representative, as the review says); or anything after 2014.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Sources: published case reports and case series, several only as congress abstracts; the EMCDDA risk assessment of 25I-NBOMe (April 2014); one poison-centre series; forensic and media reports of deaths; two surveys; Erowid and Bluelight counts (pp. 85–91).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Papers relating to prevalence of use or acute toxicity of an NBOMe drug (p. 86, Methods); no other criteria stated.
sample.selection_effects: Published case reports favour severe, unusual or analytically interesting cases: in the poison-centre series seizures were recorded in 4%, against 38% across the published case reports (p. 90). Grey literature includes a media report of a death without analytical data (p. 90). One of the two prevalence surveys is the authors' own congress abstract (Lovett, Measham, Dargan and Wood, 2014; reference 19), and the 25 non-fatal EU cases and 4 deaths come from an EMCDDA risk assessment whose extended scientific committee meeting two authors attended, the other two being EMCDDA staff (p. 85, affiliations; p. 91, Declaration of interest).

exposure.measurement: Varies by case: what the person said or what the product was labelled; analysis of remaining product (blotter, liquid, capsule) in some; detection in the patient's urine, blood or post-mortem samples in others; no analysis in several (pp. 87–91). The review states for each case whether and how the NBOMe was confirmed.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Routes in the cases: swallowed (blotters, pills, capsules), sublingual (a film, blotter), nasal and, in one case, intravenous injection of a liquid (pp. 87–89). Amounts were mostly unknown or self-reported and are not used here. The review describes 25I-NBOMe as very potent, with reported amounts taken far smaller than for mephedrone and similar to other potent hallucinogens such as LSD (p. 85).
exposure.polysubstance: Other drugs were detected or reported in many cases: amphetamine and methamphetamine in 6 of the 7 cases of the Hill series; ketamine in the second Hong Kong case; ethanol and a cannabinoid-positive immunoassay in the Richmond 25I case; caffeine in all three Grand Rapids cases tested; a PCP analogue in the Detroit case; co-use of ethanol, 2C-E, cannabis or ketamine reported by 4 of the 10 Richmond patients; cannabis metabolites in both Houston deaths; amphetamine, ketamine, lidocaine, 5-MeO-DIPT and DOI in the UK death (pp. 87–91). In the Texas series 21 of 25 (84%) reported no other substance (p. 90). The pooled percentages do not separate cases with and without other drugs.

comparison.controls: None. The review contrasts the published case reports with the Texas poison-centre series (seizures 38% against 4%, p. 90) and, within the same surveys, NBOMe use with use of mephedrone, LSD, magic mushrooms and ketamine (pp. 86–87).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not available for most cases: medical and psychiatric history, tolerance, amount taken, time from use to presentation.

outcomes.instruments: Clinical features as reported in each source (heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, seizures, agitation, hallucinations, clonus, creatine kinase, creatinine); survey questions on awareness and on lifetime, last-year and last-month use; analytical methods of the cases (LC–MS/MS, HPLC–MS/MS, GC–MS, time-of-flight MS).
outcomes.validity_norms: No definitions or thresholds are given for tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia or agitation in the pooled percentages; Table 2 marks hyperpyrexia 'Yes' for three cases whose listed temperatures are 36.5–37.3°C (p. 88).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Acute toxicity' is any reported case of harm after NBOMe use; an 'NBOMe-related death' is a death in which an NBOMe was detected or reported, whatever the cause.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical tests by the reviewers; the survey p-values are quoted from the sources).

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled effect sizes. Pooled percentages across the 29 published cases: tachycardia 96.6%, hypertension 62.0%, agitation/aggression 48.2%, seizures 37.9%, hyperthermia 27.6%; acute kidney injury in 5 patients (pp. 85, 91); these equal 28, 18, 14, 11 and 8 of 29 (editors' calculation; 14 of 29 is 48.3%). Texas poison-centre series (25 cases, 2012–2013): tachycardia 52%, agitation/irritability 48%, hallucinations 32%, hypertension 32%, confusion 24%, mydriasis 20%, seizures 4% (p. 90). Global Drugs Survey 2013: 582 of 22,289 (2.6%) had ever used 25B-, 25C- or 25I-NBOMe and 526 (2.4%) in the last 12 months, against LSD 39.4% lifetime and 15.0% last year in the same sample (p. 86). South East London nightclub survey 2013 (n = 397): lifetime NBOMe use 4.8% against 76.6% for mephedrone; last month 1.8% against 62.2% (p. 87).
analysis.selective_reporting: No list of included and excluded reports; congress abstracts and a media report are used alongside full papers; features are tabulated case by case only for the Hill series (Table 2) and the Grand Rapids cases (Table 3), so the pooled percentages cannot be traced to cases.

interpretation_gap.results_show: By late 2014, 29 published cases of NBOMe poisoning (23 with 25I-NBOMe), mostly in young men, described stimulant-like and serotonergic features (fast heart rate, high blood pressure, agitation, seizures, high temperature), with severe complications in some (status epilepticus, rhabdomyolysis with kidney injury needing dialysis or filtration, prolonged intensive care). Eight deaths had been reported, in five of which 25I-NBOMe was found on analysis; several deaths followed disturbed behaviour, and in several cases people believed they had taken LSD. A poison-centre series recorded far fewer seizures (4%) than the published cases.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that 25I-NBOMe has been detected in eight fatalities (p. 85), whereas the body reports no analytical confirmation for three of them (pp. 90–91). The abstract and conclusions say five patients developed acute kidney injury (pp. 85, 91); the case descriptions include six (editors' count). The conclusion that NBOMe use is limited compared with classical recreational drugs and mephedrone (pp. 85, 91) rests on two 2013 surveys that the review itself calls non-representative (p. 86). The body is otherwise cautious: it states case by case when exposure was not confirmed or other drugs were present, and that the role of NBOMes in the deaths has often not been determined (p. 91).

timeline.event: Hill et al. (2013): seven men with analytically confirmed 25I-NBOMe toxicity in North East England, summarized here (p. 88, Table 2). Not read.
Lawn et al. (2014): NBOMe questions in the Global Drugs Survey 2013, summarized here (p. 86). Not read.
Forrester (2014): 25 NBOMe exposures reported to Texas poison centres in 2012–2013, summarized here (p. 90). Not read.
EMCDDA risk assessment of 25I-NBOMe (April 2014): 25 non-fatal cases and 4 deaths reported to the EU Early Warning System, summarized here (pp. 89–91). Not read.
Walterscheid et al. (2014) and Poklis et al. (2014): three deaths with 25I-NBOMe found in post-mortem samples (Houston and Richmond), summarized here (pp. 90–91). Not read.
Kopra et al. (2022b), Global Drug Survey reports of emergency treatment after LSD: the authors note that NBOMes taken as LSD may account for some incidents (card sc_kopra_2022b).

replication.where_it_stands: This review gathers the case evidence on NBOMes up to 2014; its pooled figures are shares of published cases, not risks. The Texas poison-centre series it cites suggests that seizures are much less frequent among people who reach poison centres than among published cases. No study read for this card measures how often blotters sold as LSD contain NBOMes or the risk of harm per use.

funding.funder: No funding statement in the article.
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed (Declaration of interest, p. 91): DMW is an expert advisor to the UK Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs (ACMD) and to the EMCDDA; PID is a member of the ACMD and of the scientific committee of the EMCDDA; both received travel costs to attend the extended scientific committee meeting of the EMCDDA risk assessment in April 2014 at which 25I-NBOMe was discussed; RS and AC report no declarations of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: Wood and Dargan: Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust and King's Health Partners, and King's College London; Sedefov and Cunningham: EMCDDA, Lisbon (p. 85). The EMCDDA risk assessment and the authors' own nightclub survey supply part of the evidence. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective toxicovigilance of emergency presentations after use of hallucinogens sold as LSD, with laboratory confirmation of the drug and of any other drugs in the patient's own samples and a record of the clinical course, so that the frequency of seizures, hyperthermia, kidney injury and death after confirmed NBOMe exposure can be estimated and compared with LSD; together with drug-checking data on how often blotters sold as LSD contain NBOMes.

domains.note: A search is described (PubMed 1966–2014, two congresses' abstracts, the EDND, Google), but it uses one bibliographic database, states no eligibility criteria beyond relevance, and gives no flow of records or account of who selected.

No formal tool, but each case is described with whether the NBOMe was confirmed, in which sample and what else was found; the pooled percentages nonetheless mix confirmed, unconfirmed, abstract-only and multi-drug cases, without definitions.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: One of the two prevalence surveys is the authors' own congress abstract; 25 non-fatal cases and 4 deaths come from the EMCDDA risk assessment, in whose committee meeting two authors took part, the other two being EMCDDA staff; the case reports are mostly by others.

Uncertainty is flagged case by case in the body, but the abstract states that 25I-NBOMe was detected in all eight deaths (five in the body) and concludes that use is limited from two non-representative surveys.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on how harmful NBOMes are (severe published cases against milder poison-centre cases)
domains.note: The review reports the Texas poison-centre series with its 4% seizures beside the 38% of published cases, but does not discuss the selection of published cases; people who used NBOMes without coming to medical attention are not represented.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The search is described and the case-by-case reporting of analytical confirmation is careful, but selection is not explicit, the pooled percentages cannot be fully reproduced from the review's own case descriptions, and the abstract overstates the number of deaths with analytical detection. Citable for: what the published cases to 2014 recorded, given as shares of 29 published cases (for example seizures in roughly 4 of 10); the eight reported deaths and the five with 25I-NBOMe found on analysis; the cases in which people believed they had taken LSD; the Texas poison-centre series. Not citable for: the risk of seizures or death per use, causation in individual cases, or population prevalence.

key_findings.finding: Search and sources: PubMed with the term 'NBOMe' and the names of ten NBOMe compounds, 1966–2014; abstracts of the 2010–2014 EAPCCT and 2010–2013 NACCT congresses; the EMCDDA's European Information System and Database on New Drugs; a Google search for grey literature; each paper kept if it related to prevalence of use or acute toxicity.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Methods (p. 85); Methods, single paragraph (p. 85, continued on p. 86)

key_findings.finding: 29 published cases of acute toxicity associated with NBOMe use: 23 with 25I-NBOMe, 3 with 25B-NBOMe and 3 with 25C-NBOMe; no information was available on acute toxicity of 25B-N(BOMe)2, 25D-, 25E-, 25G-, 25N- or 25iP-NBOMe.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Acute toxicity (p. 85); Acute toxicity, 1st paragraph (p. 87)

key_findings.finding: Across the 29 published cases, the most commonly reported features were tachycardia (96.6%), hypertension (62.0%), agitation/aggression (48.2%), seizures (37.9%) and hyperthermia (27.6%); five patients were reported to have developed acute kidney injury.
key_findings.note: Shares of 29 published, selected cases, not risks; the features are not defined. By the editors' count of the review's own case descriptions: seizures in 12 (41.4%), not 11; agitation in about 17, not 14; acute kidney injury in 6, not 5; tachycardia in 28 agrees (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Severe complications among the published cases included status epilepticus with a rectal temperature of 40°C (25B-NBOMe), rhabdomyolysis with acute kidney injury (peak creatine kinase up to 30,000 IU/L; haemofiltration in one case, haemodialysis in two), acute lung injury needing prolonged invasive ventilation (25C-NBOMe), and a 38-day intensive-care stay after intravenous injection of a liquid labelled 25I-NBOMe, followed by discharge after 43 days with normal kidney function.
key_findings.locator: 25B-NBOMe, 3rd paragraph (p. 87); 25C-NBOMe, 1st paragraph (p. 87, continued on p. 88); 25I-NBOMe, 2nd paragraph (p. 88, continued on p. 89) and 6th paragraph (p. 89)

key_findings.finding: Hill et al. series (North East England, reported in January 2013): seven men aged 19–29; one injected a liquid labelled 25I-NBOMe bought from a drug dealer and six used purple capsules of powder bought on the Internet at a house party (three swallowed, three snorted); 25I-NBOMe was found in the urine and plasma of all seven, and amphetamine and methamphetamine in cases 2–7; seizures were recorded in 3, agitation in 5 and hyperpyrexia marked in 6; cases 3–7 were discharged from the emergency department after short observation (stays of 15 h to under 24 h).

Ten patients aged 14–20 in Richmond, Virginia (congress abstract), after swallowing or snorting '25-I': tachycardia in 9, hypertension 7, agitation 6, hallucinations 5, prolonged seizures 2, reduced consciousness 1; one with prolonged seizures had discrete haemorrhages within the brain and acute kidney injury; six were admitted to intensive care for observation. No analysis was reported in the abstract; serum from two patients, later analysed, contained 25I-NBOMe but could not be linked to particular patients.

Four men aged 18–19 in Grand Rapids, Michigan (congress abstract), after swallowing or snorting 25I-NBOMe: all tachycardic (108–184 bpm), three with prolonged seizures needing sedation and intubation, one with rhabdomyolysis (creatine kinase 30,000 IU/L) and acute kidney injury needing haemodialysis; urine from three contained 25I-NBOMe and caffeine.

Editors' count from the case descriptions: the NBOMe was found in the patient's own samples, with the result linked to the patient, in 15 of the 29 published cases (both Hong Kong cases, the Richmond 25B case, all 7 Hill cases, the Richmond 25I case, the St Paul case and 3 of the 4 Grand Rapids cases); only the product was analysed in 2 (Detroit, Burning Man); and no analysis linked to the patient was reported in 12 (the German 25C case, the 10 Richmond patients and one Grand Rapids patient).
key_findings.note: Not stated by the review, which concludes only that some of these reports included analytical confirmation (Conclusions, 1st paragraph).

key_findings.finding: Texas Poison Centers, 2012–2013: 25 NBOMe cases (8 in 2012, 17 in 2013); 19 (76%) involved 25I-NBOMe, 3 (12%) 25C-NBOMe and 3 an unidentified NBOMe; no other substance in 21 (84%); the most common effects were tachycardia (52%), agitation/irritability (48%), hallucinations (32%), hypertension (32%), confusion (24%) and mydriasis (20%); seizures were reported in 4%, against 38% across the published case reports.
key_findings.locator: NBOMe-drug-related toxicity reported to poison centres, single paragraph

key_findings.finding: 25 further cases of acute 25I-NBOMe toxicity reported to the EU Early Warning System (EMCDDA risk assessment, April 2014): 18 from Sweden (July 2012 to July 2013; 5 analytically confirmed, matrix not stated; features included mydriasis, anxiety, agitation, hallucinations, psychotic symptoms, tachycardia and hyperthermia), 4 from Poland (August 2013; no clinical information or confirmation) and 3 from Belgium (August 2013; confirmed in urine with no other drugs; brought from the same party, they reported using 'synthetic LSD').
key_findings.locator: 25I-NBOMe acute toxicity cases from the EMCDDA Risk Assessment Report, single paragraph (p. 89, continued on p. 90)

key_findings.finding: Eight deaths were reported with 25I-NBOMe, in one together with 25C-NBOMe; every published fatality with an NBOMe concerned 25I-NBOMe. Analytical detection is reported for five: two people after a rave party in Houston (post-mortem heart blood and urine), a 19-year-old in Richmond (blood, urine, vitreous humour, brain, liver and bile), a man in Belgium whose death was reported as from natural causes, and a 22-year-old man in the UK who drowned (with 25C-NBOMe and five other substances). For three (a 17-year-old in Australia known from a media report, the first Belgian death and the Polish death) no analytical confirmation was reported.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › NBOMe-related deaths (p. 85); NBOMe-related deaths, all paragraphs (pp. 90–91)
key_findings.note: The abstract says 25I-NBOMe was detected in eight fatalities; five is the editors' count from the body.

key_findings.finding: Several deaths followed disturbed behaviour: a 17-year-old in Australia was reported to act erratically and then jumped from a third-floor balcony; a 19-year-old in Richmond, not known by his friends to have taken anything while they used 'acid' blotters later found to contain 25I-NBOMe, fell or jumped from a balcony, and 25I-NBOMe was confirmed in his samples; a 21-year-old in Houston who had taken two 'hits of acid' hallucinated, injured himself and attacked a friend before being found unresponsive. A 15-year-old who drank an unknown clear liquid was in asystole and hyperthermic (39.9°C) on arrival. The post-mortem examinations of the two Houston deaths showed only external injuries.
key_findings.locator: NBOMe-related deaths, 2nd–6th paragraphs (p. 90, the 6th continued on p. 91)

key_findings.finding: How NBOMes were sold or mistaken: typically on blotters, also as powder and liquid. People in several cases believed they had taken LSD: a woman at the Burning Man festival had taken 'acid' on blotter paper whose remains contained mainly 25C-NBOMe with a very small amount of 25I-NBOMe; the three Belgian cases reported 'synthetic LSD'; a man who died in Houston had taken two 'hits of acid'; a Belgian who died had used a blotter believed to contain LSD, and no LSD was found; in Richmond, friends' 'acid' blotters contained 25I-NBOMe. Other forms: a liquid labelled 25I-NBOMe from a dealer, capsules bought online, an 'NBOMe' pill, a sublingual 'Holland film', and an eye dropper said to hold 2C-T-2 or 2C-T-7 that held 2C-NBOMe variants and a PCP analogue. By the editors' count of Table 1 (p. 86), 8 of the 10 first detections in Europe in 2011–2013 were on blotters, alone or with powder.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 1st paragraph (p. 85); Table 1 (p. 86); 25B-NBOMe, 1st–2nd paragraphs (p. 87); 25C-NBOMe, 2nd–3rd paragraphs (p. 88); 25I-NBOMe, 2nd paragraph (p. 88); EMCDDA cases (pp. 89–90); NBOMe-related deaths (pp. 90–91)

key_findings.finding: Global Drugs Survey 2013 (22,289 respondents, mainly from the UK and USA, asked about 25B-, 25C- and 25I-NBOMe): 582 (2.6%) had ever used one; 25I-NBOMe most often (442; 2.0% of all respondents and 75.9% of those who had used an NBOMe); 526 (2.4%) in the last 12 months, 296 (56.7%) of them in the USA and 111 (21.3%) in the UK. Lifetime and last-year use in the same sample: LSD 39.4% and 15.0%, magic mushrooms 43.1% and 16.1%, ketamine 26.0% and 11.2%.

South East London nightclub survey, summer 2013 (397 participants, 89% male, 75% men who have sex with men; NBOMes asked about as a class): 11.8% had heard of NBOMes against 96.0% for mephedrone; lifetime use 4.8% against 76.6%; last-month use 1.8% against 62.2% (all p < 0.001); awareness and use did not differ between men who have sex with men and other participants.
key_findings.locator: Prevalence of use, 4th paragraph (p. 86, continued on p. 87)
key_findings.note: One of the two surveys, published as a congress abstract by Lovett, Measham, Dargan and Wood (reference 19); the review calls both surveys non-representative (p. 86).

key_findings.finding: Other indicators: Erowid held 314 reports of NBOMe use, rising from 5 in 2010 to 148 in 2012 and 126 in the first half of 2013, and more than 8,000 posts on the Bluelight forum contained the word 'NBOMe'; in September 2014 the UNODC reported 25I-NBOMe as the most frequently reported new psychoactive substance, accounting for 43% of all cases reported to it in 2014 from 23 countries and territories.
key_findings.locator: Prevalence of use, 1st paragraph (p. 86) and 5th paragraph (p. 87)

key_findings.finding: The review describes 25I-NBOMe as a very potent 5-HT2A receptor agonist (Ki 0.044–0.15, printed in nm), with reported amounts taken far smaller than for mephedrone and similar to those of other potent hallucinogens such as LSD.

The authors conclude that NBOMe use appears limited compared with classical recreational drugs and mephedrone; that the case reports suggest both serotonin syndrome and sympathomimetic toxicity, much like MDMA, certain other amphetamines and mephedrone; that the significance of post-mortem detection for the deaths has often not been determined; and that clinicians should seek analytical confirmation in acute toxicity.

reporting_issues.issue: Global Drugs Survey: 65 respondents who used 25C-NBOMe are given as 0.8% of the whole cohort and 11.3% of those who had used an NBOMe. Editors' calculation: 65 of 22,289 is 0.29%, and 11.3% of 582 is 66.
reporting_issues.consequence: About 0.3% of respondents, not 0.8%, reported 25C-NBOMe use; minor.

reporting_issues.issue: The 526 respondents who used an NBOMe in the last 12 months are given as 91% of those who had ever used one, and the country breakdown as 296, 111, 53, 51 and 11 with percentages of 56.7, 21.3, 10.2, 9.8 and 2.1. Editors' calculation: 526 of 582 is 90.4%; the five countries add to 522, and the percentages are of 522, not 526.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; four respondents are missing from the country breakdown.

reporting_issues.issue: The pooled feature percentages (abstract and conclusions) are not reproducible from the review's own descriptions of the 29 cases, and the features are not defined. Editors' count: seizures in 12 (the first Hong Kong case, the Richmond 25B case, the German 25C case, Hill cases 1, 2 and 4, the St Paul case, 2 of the 10 Richmond patients and 3 of the 4 Grand Rapids patients), that is 41.4%, against 37.9% (11 of 29) printed; agitation in about 17, against 14 (48.2% printed, although 14 of 29 is 48.3%); acute kidney injury in 6 (the second Hong Kong case, the Richmond 25B case, the German case, Hill case 1, one Richmond patient and one Grand Rapids patient), against five; tachycardia in 28 of 29 agrees with 96.6%. Hypertension and hyperthermia have no stated thresholds and cannot be checked.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite these features as approximate shares of published cases (for example seizures in roughly 4 of 10), not as precise percentages; the primary reports may hold details that the review's summaries leave out.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 marks hyperpyrexia 'Yes' for Hill cases 4, 6 and 7, whose listed temperatures are 37.3, 36.5 and 36.9°C.
reporting_issues.consequence: The listed temperatures may be at presentation rather than peak values, or the flags may be wrong; either way the pooled hyperthermia share is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that 25I-NBOMe has been detected in eight fatalities, but the body reports no analytical confirmation for three of them (the Australian media report, the first Belgian death and the Polish death).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite as reported in eight deaths and found on analysis in five.

reporting_issues.issue: Mis-citations: Table 2 is titled as the cases reported by Hill et al. with reference 30, which is Stellpflug et al.; Hill et al. is reference 31. Table 3 cites reference 34, an analytical-method paper by Poklis et al., for the four Grand Rapids cases, which the text attributes to reference 35 (Kelly et al.).
reporting_issues.consequence: Trace these cases by author and place, not by the review's reference numbers.

reporting_issues.issue: 25H-NBOMe is said to have been detected at a concentration below the lower limit of detection (25H-NBOMe section), while the St Paul case reports it below the lower limit of quantitation with an estimated value (25I-NBOMe section, 4th paragraph). One Belgian case's blood pressure is printed as 150/8 mmHg, an impossible value.
The UNODC figure is given as 25I-NBOMe accounting for 43% of all cases reported to it in 2014, from 23 countries and territories, without saying cases of what (detections, notifications or seizures).
reporting_issues.consequence: Do not cite the 43% as a share of seizures or of drug use without reading the UNODC source.

Born-digital text layer; the download stamp in the margin is not part of the article. No funding statement; no supplement; no companion paper named in the list row. The reference record agrees with the PDF (title, four authors, 2015, volume 53, issue 2, pages 85–92). Locators count running-text paragraphs within each section or subsection; tables are not counted.
